title.text: Workflow mapping (practical)

objects.text: Which of my tasks should be a rule, an AI step or an agent?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 12 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 12, the first of three practical sessions. Last time, in Session 11, we watched an agent work inside written permissions, with human-in-the-loop approval before anything that cannot be undone. Today the mode changes. For eleven sessions I mostly demonstrated and you watched. From today you do the work, on one task of your own, from work or the summary of your own email, and I work beside you.

We map it, decide what kind of help each step needs, and estimate the hours you could save. Our question is this: which of my tasks should be a rule, an AI step or an agent?

objects.text: By the end of today you will have

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.70.png

slides.notes:
You answer that question for your own work, and you leave with three things made by your own hand. A map of one workflow of your own: what starts it, the steps, the handoffs and the check. A choice for every step: rule-based automation, an AI step, an agent or a person, with a sketch of a personal assistant if one fits.

And a baseline and an hours-saved estimate in the Business Case Workbook, with the net benefit, payback period and ROI. The clock shows how much of today is yours.

title.text:
Your two hours: 55 minutes
are your own workflow

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_dc706388.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Most of today is your own work, with me at your side.

slides.notes:
This is the first practical, and the clock shows it. After ten minutes of recall, twenty-five minutes on the idea: a workflow and automation, first at home with tea and a bank standing order, then at work, and how to decide each step and price the change with a baseline, net benefit, payback period and ROI.

Ten minutes of demonstration: a recorded AI sort and a keyword rule on the same twelve messages. Then, after a short break, fifty-five minutes on your own workflow. We end with a decision on what to build first. First, the recall.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What are the three steps of the agent loop?
2.  Which four kinds of action must always wait for human-in-the-loop approval?
3.  What are the four rows of the Tool Boundary Sheet, the permissions table?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 11. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What are the three steps of the agent loop? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Plan the next step, act by calling one tool, observe the result, and repeat until the goal is met or a stop condition fires.

Question two. Which four kinds of action must always wait for human-in-the-loop approval? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Sends, payments, deletions and commitments such as accepting a price.

Question three. What are the four rows of the Tool Boundary Sheet, the permissions table? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. Read, write, send and spend. For each: what it may do, what a person approves and what it must never do.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text:
How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_a0e3bad5.png
objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold agents, permissions and approval from Session 11 and a baseline to beat from Session 3. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: workflow mapped; baseline, net benefit, payback.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 13: the rules and questions around that choice. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A task that repeats, from the event that starts it to the result someone checks.
The event that starts a workflow, such as an alarm, a date or a message arriving.
A machine runs fixed rules with no judgement, such as a bank standing order.
How long the task takes, what it costs and how often it goes wrong today, measured before you change anything.
Net benefit: gains minus all costs. Return on investment (ROI): net benefit divided by cost.
How long until the savings repay the one-off cost: one-off cost divided by the saving a month.

slides.notes:
6 words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Workflow. A task that repeats, from the event that starts it to the result someone checks.

Trigger. The event that starts a workflow, such as an alarm, a date or a message arriving.

Rule-based automation. A machine runs fixed rules with no judgement, such as a bank standing order.

Baseline. How long the task takes, what it costs and how often it goes wrong today, measured before you change anything.

Net benefit and ROI. Net benefit: gains minus all costs. Return on investment (ROI): net benefit divided by cost.

Payback period. How long until the savings repay the one-off cost: one-off cost divided by the saving a month.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
Everyday first: making tea is a workflow
with a trigger, steps, a handoff and a check

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_tea_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Everyday first: making tea is a workflow with a trigger, steps, a handoff and a check

objects.text: Every workflow has four parts. You already run one each morning.

runs.text: Trigger: what starts it.
Steps: what is done, in order.
Handoff: where work changes hands.
Check: who confirms the result.

slides.notes:
Of today’s words, workflow is the one the session hangs on, so we start with one you know. Making morning tea. The trigger is the alarm at half past six. Then the steps, in order: boil the water, brew for three minutes, add milk and sugar. Then a handoff: the cup passes from you to the person who drinks it.

And the check: they taste it. If the tea is cold, the delay was probably at that handoff. Every workflow, at home or at work, has the same four parts: trigger, steps, handoffs and a check. If you can name these four for a task, you can decide where a machine fits.

So when does a machine run a workflow on its own?

title.text:
Rule-based automation runs fixed rules
without you: a bank standing order

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_standing_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Rule-based automation runs fixed rules without you: a bank standing order

objects.text: Automation means a machine runs the workflow. Rule-based automation follows fixed rules.

runs.text: Trigger: the 25th of each month.
Rule: pay UGX 500,000 to the landlord.
Check: you read the statement.

slides.notes:
A machine already runs one of your workflows. Automation means a machine carries out the steps when the trigger fires, without you. The simplest kind is rule-based automation: fixed rules with no judgement. A bank standing order is a good example. The trigger is a date, the twenty-fifth of each month.

The rule is fixed: pay UGX 500,000 to the landlord. The bank never decides whether the landlord deserves it. Your part is the check, reading the statement, and when the rent changes, you change the rule. That is a person in the loop, as in Session 11. Rules suit steps with clear words or numbers. Now the same four parts at work.

title.text:
Where you see it at work: customer
messages at Nile Valley Foods in three lanes

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_map_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Where you see it at work: customer messages at Nile Valley Foods in three lanes

objects.text: One lane per person or team. Red arrows are handoffs: Customer Service waits for Finance.

slides.notes:
Here is a finished map from our case company. A customer message is a short text, such as an order, a payment notice or a complaint, and the company wants each one answered by the right team. Each lane is a person or a team. The trigger, in red, is a customer message arriving.

Customer Service reads and sorts it, then drafts a reply. When money is involved, the draft waits for Finance to confirm the payment: that handoff and its return are the red arrows. Finally a person checks and sends. Draw your own map the same way: lanes for people, boxes for steps, arrows for handoffs.

Once the map is drawn, the question becomes what kind of help each box needs.

title.text: Decide each step with four questions

rows.text: Is the answer fixed by clear words or numbers?
A payment reference goes to Finance
Does it need the meaning of text, with a quick check?
Sort a polite complaint; draft a reply
Does it need several tools and its own next step?
Read a mailbox and draft replies
Does money, trust or law turn on it?
Approve a credit; send the reply

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_robot_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_person_0.50.png

objects.text: Ask the questions in this order. Use the first answer that fits.

slides.notes:
To answer that, ask four questions of each step on your map, in order. Is the answer fixed by clear words or numbers?

Then use rule-based automation, like the standing order, or a payment reference that always goes to Finance. Does it need the meaning of the text, and can a person check the result quickly?

Then an AI step: one model call inside a fixed path. Does it need several tools and a choice of next step?

Then an agent, with the permissions table from Session 11. And whenever money, trust or the law turns on the step, a person decides: human-in-the-loop. Use the first answer that fits. Let me apply the four questions to the map you just saw.

title.text: The same map with a choice on every step

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_map_11.90x4.25_3beb07f1.png
objects.alt: The same map with a choice on every step

objects.text: Two AI steps, one rule and a person at the end. No step here needs a full agent.

slides.notes:
Here is the same map with those questions answered on each step. Reading and sorting is an AI step, because meaning matters: a polite complaint has no angry words. Drafting is an AI step too. Confirming a payment is rule-based, because a payment reference is clear. Checking and sending stays with a person, because a reply commits the company.

Notice that no step needs a full agent. Most workflows need one or two AI steps inside a fixed path. An agent earns its place only when the steps change from case to case. These choices are claims, though, so let me test the two cheapest kinds on real messages.

title.text:
Demonstration: the rule and the AI on
the same twelve customer messages

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_606a0631.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: the rule and the AI on the same twelve customer messages

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Which messages fool the rule?
Which one fools the AI?
What does UNSURE cost you?
What was never measured?

slides.notes:
Here is that test, rule-based automation and the AI side by side, from records we already have; nothing is rerun. The AI sort is a recorded run you see for the first time today; Session 2 only mentioned it. The rule is a simple keyword router I wrote after reading the twelve messages, so its seven flatters it.

The rule sends messages to queues by words: payment words to Finance, late or delay to Customer Service, everything else to the Sales desk. The AI reads the meaning and picks a category, or says UNSURE. Both are scored against the answer key. Watch which messages fool the rule, which one fools the AI, and what the UNSURE answers cost a person.

title.text:
Side by side: the rule routes 7 of 12, the
AI sorts 9 exactly and 11 acceptably

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_side_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Side by side: the rule routes 7 of 12, the AI sorts 9 exactly and 11 acceptably

objects.text: AI: Claude, three fresh sessions, 4 November 2026; not ChatGPT or Gemini. Rule: computed.

slides.notes:
So which messages fooled the rule, and which one fooled the AI?

Here are the twelve, side by side. The rule gets seven right. It fails on M03, wet sugar with no keyword, on M10, a polite complaint, on M32, sarcastic thanks, and on M07 and M38, where late is part of an ordinary order. The AI, in three fresh Claude sessions on the fourth of November, gets nine exactly right and says UNSURE on two, which is acceptable. It is wrong on M14, which it called a complaint while Finance must act first. The two counts use different measures, so read them side by side. And the time a person takes to check the AI was never measured.

title.text:
A personal assistant is a small workflow:
sketch its inputs, outputs and approval step

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_assistant_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A personal assistant is a small workflow: sketch its inputs, outputs and approval step

objects.text: Your own email is a good first workflow to map.

runs.text: Trigger: every morning at 7.
Permissions: read one mailbox, write drafts.
Human-in-the-loop: you send every reply.

slides.notes:
Before we count hours, here is a workflow closer to home: your own inbox. Many executives would most like help with their own email, and that is a workflow too. Sketch it like this. The trigger is the time, every morning at seven. The inputs are one mailbox and your rules, such as who counts as urgent.

The outputs are a summary and draft replies. The permissions are read and draft, autonomy level two from Session 11. And you are the human in the loop: it never sends, pays or deletes. If you prefer a work task, map that instead. The sketch is the same. Next we count what a workflow saves, starting again at home.

title.text:
Everyday first: baseline, payback period,
net benefit and ROI for an electric kettle

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_kettle_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Everyday first: baseline, payback period, net benefit and ROI for an electric kettle

objects.text: Measure today first, then price the change. Invented round numbers.

runs.text: Payback period = set-up cost ÷ net saving a month.
Net benefit = benefits − costs.
ROI = net benefit ÷ cost × 100%.

slides.notes:
Here are the four money words on something at home. You make tea on charcoal and think of buying an electric kettle. First the baseline: charcoal for tea costs you UGX 30,000 a month today, measured before any change. With the kettle, electricity costs UGX 10,000, so the saving is UGX 20,000 a month.

The kettle costs UGX 60,000 once. Payback period: sixty thousand divided by twenty thousand, three months. Net benefit in the first year: twelve times twenty thousand, minus sixty thousand, is UGX 180,000. Return on investment, ROI, is net benefit divided by cost, times one hundred percent: one hundred and eighty thousand over sixty thousand, three hundred percent. These are invented numbers. Now the same method at work.

title.text:
At work, measure the baseline first: the saving
is the gap between today and the new way

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_hours_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: At work, measure the baseline first: the saving is the gap between today and the new way

objects.text: Hours saved = runs a month × minutes saved per run ÷ 60.

runs.text: Before review: 320 minutes, 5.3 hours a month.
After 20 minutes of review a run: 240 minutes, 4 hours.
Invented NVF plan numbers.

slides.notes:
At work the baseline is the same idea as in Session 3, the score to beat: how long the task takes today, measured before you change anything. Take the Monday sales email at Nile Valley Foods, a weekly summary of sales sent to managers. Today it takes ninety minutes. With the new routine the plan is ten minutes of your own work, so each run saves eighty minutes before review time. It runs four times a month. Hours saved equals runs a month times minutes saved per run, divided by sixty: four times eighty is three hundred and twenty minutes, about five point three hours.

But a person reviews each run for twenty minutes, so the real saving is sixty minutes a run: four times sixty is two hundred and forty minutes, four hours. The workbook prices review as a running cost. Invented plan numbers.

title.text:
The Business Case Workbook turns hours
into net benefit, payback period and ROI

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t12_money_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The Business Case Workbook turns hours into net benefit, payback period and ROI

objects.text: Gains minus running cost gives the net benefit a month.

runs.text: Net benefit = benefits − costs = 304,000 − 145,000 = UGX 159,000 a month.
Payback period = 480,000 ÷ 159,000 ≈ 3.0 months.

slides.notes:
Hours persuade you; money persuades whoever holds the budget. These are the grey example values in the workbook, invented for Nile Valley Foods, and I recomputed them from its own formulas. Time saved, 320 minutes at UGX 30,000 an hour, is UGX 160,000 a month. Errors avoided add UGX 144,000.

The running cost is UGX 145,000, including review time. Net benefit is benefits minus costs: UGX 159,000 a month. Payback period is set-up cost divided by net a month: 480,000 over 159,000, about three months. Over the first year the net is twelve times 159,000 minus the set-up, UGX 1,428,000, against total costs of UGX 2,220,000: an ROI of sixty-four percent. After a five-minute break, you start mapping.

title.text:
Map your workflow: trigger,
steps, handoffs and check

objects.text: 15 minutes
Your own workflow
Draw one repeated task in lanes, from trigger to check.

runs.text: Pick one weekly task. Unsure? List options on the Use-Case Scorecard.
Draw one lane for each person or system.
Write the trigger, then each step in a box.
Mark every handoff in red and the check in gold.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_5.50x3.55_3557777c.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A one-page map of your workflow with the handoffs marked.

slides.notes:
Welcome back. From here to the decision the work is yours, and I am at your side. Pick one task you do every week. It can be a work task, such as the monthly report, supplier invoices or leave requests, or the summary of your own email. Draw a lane for each person or system involved.

Write the trigger, then each step in a box, as we did for the tea. Mark every handoff in red and the check in gold. If you cannot choose, list a few on the Ten tasks sheet of the Use-Case Scorecard: task, owner, how often, kind of work and minutes each time.

Then fill the top of a Task Card. You have fifteen minutes.

title.text:
Decide each step: rule-based
automation, AI step, agent or person

objects.text: 15 minutes
Your own workflow
Tag every box on your map with one choice and one reason.

runs.text: Ask the four questions for each step, in order.
Write rule, AI step, agent or person in the box.
For each AI step, write how a person checks it.
Circle the step that costs the most time.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_251ccb84.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: Your map with a choice, a reason and a check on every step.

slides.notes:
With your map drawn, the second step is to decide, using the four questions from earlier. For every box on your map, ask them in order. Clear words or numbers: rule-based automation. Meaning with a quick check: an AI step. Several tools and its own next step: an agent.

Money, trust or law: a person. Write the choice and one reason in the box. For every AI step, write how a person checks it, because Session 10 showed us that models fail. Then circle the step that costs you the most time. That is usually where to start. You have fifteen minutes, and I keep coming round.

title.text:
Sketch your personal assistant with
its permissions and approval step

objects.text: 10 minutes
Your own workflow
Draw one assistant for your workflow: inputs, outputs, permissions, approval.

runs.text: Write its trigger and its inputs.
Write the outputs it hands to you.
Grant the fewest permissions that work.
Name who approves and the off switch.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_a2536135.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A sketch of one assistant with its four permission rows.

slides.notes:
Some of your boxes may now say AI step or agent, and this third step, ten minutes, turns them into an assistant sketch. Write its trigger and its inputs, then the outputs it hands to you. Grant the fewest permissions that still do the job, the principle of least privilege, using the four rows of the Tool Boundary Sheet: read, write, send and spend.

Name the person who approves and the off switch. If no step in your workflow suits an assistant, write that down. It is a useful finding. A rule or one AI step may be all you need. Either way, the next question is what it is worth.

title.text:
Estimate the hours saved and enter
them in the Business Case Workbook

objects.text: 15 minutes
Your own workflow
Fill the Inputs sheet for your workflow and read the hours saved and the payback period.

runs.text: Type how often, minutes today and people involved: your baseline.
Type minutes with the new routine and review minutes.
Add your hourly cost: pay plus contributions, over hours worked.
Mark each figure E for estimate or M for measured.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_177a7077.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: Your Inputs sheet filled, with the hours saved and every figure marked E or M.

slides.notes:
To put a number on it, the last step, fifteen minutes, is the workbook. Open the Business Case Workbook and go to the Inputs sheet. Type over the grey example: times a month, minutes each time today and people involved, which together are your baseline. Then minutes with the new routine and review minutes.

Never set review to zero. Work out your hourly cost: pay plus employer contributions and benefits, divided by hours worked. Mark each figure E if it is your estimate and M if you measured it. The Benefits and Result sheets then show the hours saved, the net a month and the payback period. I come round to check your figures with you.

title.text:
Plan against measurement: four
numbers to record for four weeks

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_clock_0.70.png

objects.text: Minutes each run, with the new routine, including review.

Cases sent to a person, such as the UNSURE answers we saw from the AI. And your stop rule, written now while you are calm: for example, revise if review rises above thirty minutes a run. Your map, your choices, your sketch and your estimate are all on the desk, so decide. For your mapped workflow, what do you build or test first?

Rule-based automation, when the words or numbers are clear: cheap to build and easy to explain. One AI step, when meaning matters and a person checks each result. An assistant at autonomy level two, when several steps change from case to case, with drafts only and you approving. Or measure first, when you have no baseline yet.
